name: Cryptography Basics
author: Recurse
subject: security
description: Symmetric and public-key encryption, hashing, password storage, signatures, certificates, TLS and the mistakes that break them.

lesson.intro: Cryptography protects HTTPS, passwords, software updates, messaging and payments. You should not invent algorithms, but you must know which tool solves which problem and how each fails: encryption, hashing, password storage, signatures, TLS and the classic mistakes.
objectives: Choose between symmetric and public-key encryption, hashes, MACs and signatures
Explain why passwords need salted, slow hashes such as Argon2id or bcrypt
Describe how certificates and the chain of trust let a browser trust a key
Walk through Diffie-Hellman and the TLS 1.3 handshake, including forward secrecy
Spot homemade crypto, ECB, nonce reuse, MD5, weak randomness and skipped certificate checks

sections.title: What cryptography is for
sections.key: Encryption gives confidentiality, hashes and MACs give integrity, and MACs or signatures give authenticity; the algorithms are public, so all the secrecy lives in the key.
sections.body:
The padlock in your browser, an app login, a software update: each time, cryptography answers three questions. Can anyone else read this? Has it been changed? Did it really come from who it claims?

[[visual]]

**Kerckhoffs's principle**: a system must stay secure even if everything except the key is public. AES, RSA and SHA-256 are published and have survived decades of attack. A "secret algorithm" is a red flag.

So **don't roll your own**: no homemade algorithms, and no homemade protocols assembled from primitives. A reused nonce, a missing check or a timing difference breaks schemes that look fine. Use vetted libraries: `cryptography` or PyNaCl in Python, Web Crypto or libsodium in JavaScript, TLS for data in transit.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Goals and tools
rows: **Confidentiality**
Can anyone else read it?
**Encryption** (AES, RSA): a **key** turns **plaintext** into **ciphertext** and back
**Integrity**
Has it been changed?
**Hash** or **MAC** (SHA-256, HMAC)
**Authenticity**
Who really sent it?
A MAC (shared key) or a **digital signature**
**Non-repudiation**
Can the sender deny it?
A digital signature: only the signer holds the private key

items.title: Encoding
points: Only changes how data is written
No key: anyone can reverse it

sections.pitfall: Inventing a clever scheme, such as XOR with a secret word or a custom cipher. Homemade cryptography fails in ways its author cannot see; use a vetted library.

check.question: Why is it fine that the AES algorithm is completely public?
choices: Public algorithms run slower, so attackers give up
Its security depends only on keeping the key secret
Attackers are not allowed to read the specification
AES quietly changes its algorithm every year
check.explanation: Kerckhoffs's principle: a well-designed cipher stays secure even when the attacker knows exactly how it works. Publishing it lets experts search for weaknesses, which is how trust is earned.

sections.title: Symmetric encryption
sections.key: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key and does nearly all bulk encryption; use an AEAD mode such as AES-GCM with a fresh nonce per message, and never ECB.
sections.body:
To encrypt a backup before uploading it, use **symmetric encryption**: one secret key both encrypts and decrypts. It is fast (often gigabytes per second), so it does nearly all bulk encryption: disks, files, and the data inside every TLS and VPN connection.

The standard is **AES** (128- or 256-bit keys, far beyond brute force); **ChaCha20** suits phones without AES hardware. AES is a **block cipher** on 16-byte blocks, so a **mode of operation** decides how a message is processed:

[[visual]]

AEAD modes take a **nonce** ("number used once"), usually 12 bytes. It need not be secret, but it must **never repeat** under the same key: reuse can expose plaintexts and let attackers forge messages.

[[code]]

The catch is the **key distribution problem**: both sides must already share the key. How do you agree on one with a website you have never visited?

visual.title: Modes of operation
rows: ECB
Each block encrypted alone: identical blocks give identical ciphertext, so patterns leak (an ECB-encrypted image is still recognizable). Never use it
CBC, CTR
Patterns hidden, but confidentiality only: an attacker can modify the ciphertext undetected
**AEAD**: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305
Confidentiality and integrity: decryption fails loudly if a single bit changed. Use these

sections.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)  # keep secret
aes = AESGCM(key)

nonce = os.urandom(12)        # fresh for every message
ct = aes.encrypt(nonce, b"backup data", None)

# Store nonce + ct. Decrypting also checks integrity:
pt = aes.decrypt(nonce, ct, None)  # InvalidTag if altered
sections.pitfall: Using a fixed nonce, or a counter that restarts, with AES-GCM. A repeated nonce under the same key breaks both secrecy and integrity; generate a fresh random one per message.

check.question: Which mode should new code use when encrypting data with AES?
choices: ECB, because it is the simplest
CBC, without any integrity check
No mode at all; AES handles any length by itself
An authenticated mode such as GCM
check.explanation: AEAD modes like GCM encrypt and detect tampering in one step. ECB leaks patterns, unauthenticated CBC can be modified undetected, and AES on its own only encrypts single 16-byte blocks.

sections.title: Asymmetric encryption
sections.key: Public-key cryptography gives each party a key pair: anyone encrypts with your public key and only your private key decrypts, so strangers can share secrets.
sections.body:
In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman asked: what if the locking key and the unlocking key were different? **Asymmetric** (public-key) cryptography gives each party a **key pair**: a **public key** shared with the world and a **private key** that never leaves its owner. Deriving the private key from the public one is infeasible.

[[visual]]

The main families are **RSA** (built on factoring huge numbers; use at least 2048-bit keys) and **elliptic-curve** cryptography such as X25519 and Ed25519 (similar security from 256-bit keys, and faster).

Asymmetric operations are far slower than AES, and RSA can only encrypt messages shorter than its key. So real systems, TLS included, use **hybrid encryption**:

[[visual 2]]

One question remains: how do you know a public key is really Bob's? An attacker who slips in their own key can read everything meant for him. Certificates answer that.

items.title: Encrypting for Bob
points: Strangers can send Bob secrets without ever meeting him

visual.title: Hybrid encryption: a 2 GB file for Bob

steps.label: Encrypt the file with AES-GCM and that key
Encrypt the AES key with Bob's public key
Bob decrypts the AES key with his private key, then the file

sections.pitfall: "Encrypting" a secret with your own private key. Anyone with your public key, which is everyone, can undo it; that operation is for signatures, not secrecy.

check.question: Asymmetric cryptography mainly solves which problem?
choices: Sharing secrets with someone you have never exchanged a key with
Encrypting large files faster than AES can
Compressing data before it is sent over a network
Making hash functions reversible with a key
check.explanation: Anyone can use a public key, so strangers can establish secrets without meeting first. It is much slower than AES, which is why it is used to set up a symmetric key rather than to encrypt bulk data.

sections.title: Hash functions
sections.key: A cryptographic hash turns any input into a fixed-size, one-way fingerprint; use SHA-256 or better, and an HMAC when two parties need a keyed integrity check.
sections.body:
A Linux download page lists a SHA-256 value beside each file. Hash your 3 GB copy and compare: a match means every bit arrived intact. A **cryptographic hash function** turns input of any size into a fixed-size **digest**: SHA-256 always gives 256 bits, written as 64 hex characters.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A plain hash proves integrity only if the hash comes from a trusted place, such as an HTTPS page: an attacker who swaps a file can swap a hash sent beside it.

Two parties who share a secret use an **HMAC**, a hash with a secret key mixed in, so nobody without the key can produce a valid one. Payment webhook signatures are HMACs.

[[code]]

visual.title: What a good hash guarantees
rows: Deterministic
The same input always gives the same digest
Avalanche
Changing one input bit flips about half the output bits
**Preimage resistant**
From a digest you cannot find an input. One-way: no key, no "decrypting" a hash
**Collision resistant**
You cannot find any two different inputs with the same digest, though infinitely many exist

items.title: Broken for collisions
points: Researchers have made different files with identical digests
A 2008 MD5 collision forged a rogue CA certificate
Fine for accidental corruption, never against an attacker

sections.code:
import hashlib, hmac

data = b"invoice 1042: pay $500 to ACME"
print(hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest())  # 64 hex chars

secret = b"shared-webhook-secret"
tag = hmac.new(secret, data, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

# The receiver recomputes the tag with the same secret
# and compares in constant time:
expected = hmac.new(secret, data, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(hmac.compare_digest(tag, expected))  # True
sections.deeper:
**Hashes are everywhere.** Git names every commit by a hash of its contents. Signatures sign a hash of the document rather than the document itself. Blockchains chain hashes together so that changing an old block changes every hash after it.

**Why collisions matter more than preimages.** Nobody can turn an MD5 digest back into its input, but that is not the threat. An attacker who can craft two documents with one digest can get the harmless one signed and then present the malicious one with the same valid signature.
sections.pitfall: Calling hashing "encryption", or trying to decrypt a hash. Hashes are one-way and keyless; if you need the data back, you need encryption.

activity.title: The avalanche effect
activity.prompt: Run it and compare the three digests: one extra character or one capital letter changes the whole output. Then hash a long sentence of your own and check that the digest is still 64 characters.

props.code:
import hashlib

for text in ["hello", "hello!", "Hello"]:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"{text:8}{digest}")

print(len(digest), "hex characters")
props.task: Add a long sentence of your own to the list and check its digest length.

check.question: A payment provider and your server share a secret. Which tool lets your server confirm a webhook really came from the provider and was not altered?
choices: A plain SHA-256 of the request body
Base64 encoding of the request body
An HMAC of the body computed with the shared secret
An MD5 checksum sent alongside the body
check.explanation: Anyone can compute a plain hash or a checksum of a forged body, and Base64 is just encoding. Only someone who knows the secret can produce a matching HMAC, so a valid tag proves both origin and integrity.

sections.title: Storing passwords: salts and slow hashes
sections.key: Store passwords as salted, deliberately slow hashes such as Argon2id or bcrypt, never as plaintext, encrypted text or a fast hash.
sections.body:
Breaches happen, and the password table is the prize. What attackers find depends on how you stored it:

[[visual]]

A **salt** is random, unique per user, stored beside the hash and mixed into it. It is not secret: it makes identical passwords hash differently, defeats precomputed tables and forces per-user cracking.

**Slowness** is the other half. **Argon2id** (the current recommendation), **bcrypt**, **scrypt** and **PBKDF2** have a tunable **work factor**: a quarter-second hash barely slows a login but cripples guessing. Argon2id and scrypt are also **memory-hard**, which blunts GPUs. Raise the cost as hardware improves; each +1 of bcrypt's cost doubles the work.

[[visual 2]]

Libraries generate the salt and pack algorithm, settings and salt into one stored string:

[[code]]

visual.title: Stored as...
rows: Plaintext
Every account at once, plus other sites where users reused the password
Encrypted
The key lives on the same servers, so stealing both returns every password. The server never needs the original
A fast hash (SHA-256)
One GPU tries billions of guesses a second. Without a salt, equal passwords share a hash and **rainbow tables** make cracking a lookup
**A salted, slow hash**
Each user cracked separately, at a handful of guesses per second per core

steps.label: Sign-up: generate a random salt for the user
Hash password and salt with a slow function such as Argon2id
Store the salt and the hash, never the password
Login: hash the attempt with the stored salt and settings
Compare the result with the stored hash

sections.code:
import bcrypt

# Sign-up: gensalt() makes a random salt, cost 12
stored = bcrypt.hashpw(b"correct horse", bcrypt.gensalt())
# b'$2b$12$' + 22-char salt + 31-char hash

# Login: checkpw reads salt and cost from stored
bcrypt.checkpw(b"correct horse", stored)   # True
bcrypt.checkpw(b"Correct horse", stored)   # False
sections.deeper:
**Defense around the hash.** A hash is only as strong as the passwords behind it, so also rate-limit login attempts, reject passwords known from breaches, and offer multi-factor authentication.

**Pepper.** Some systems add a pepper: a secret key kept outside the database, for example in a hardware security module, mixed into every hash. A database dump alone is then not enough to start guessing.

**Upgrading old hashes.** When you raise the work factor, re-hash each user's password with the new settings the next time they log in successfully, since that is the only moment you have the plaintext.
sections.pitfall: Treating a salt as a secret, or using one salt for every user. The salt's job is uniqueness, not secrecy; a shared salt lets one cracking run cover everyone.

check.question: What does the work factor (cost) in bcrypt or Argon2 control?
choices: The length of the stored salt
How expensive each hash is to compute, which slows guessing
How many users can log in at the same time
The maximum password length that is allowed
check.explanation: The work factor sets how much computation (and for Argon2, memory) each hash takes. Every guess an attacker makes pays the same price, so raising it makes cracking proportionally slower.

sections.title: Digital signatures, certificates and PKI
sections.key: A signature is a hash transformed with the signer's private key and checked with their public key; certificates bind public keys to names through a chain of trust.
sections.body:
Your laptop installs an operating system update that will run with full privileges. How does it know the update came from the vendor, unaltered? It checks a **digital signature**.

[[visual]]

A signature gives integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation, but **not** confidentiality: a signed email is readable by anyone unless it is also encrypted.

You still need the right public key. A **certificate** binds a public key to an identity, "this key belongs to `www.example.com`, valid March to June", and is signed by a **certificate authority** (CA) that checked the requester controls that domain.

[[visual 2]]

The browser verifies every signature up to a root in its **trust store**, then checks the hostname, the validity dates and revocation. The whole system is **PKI** (public key infrastructure). Free, auto-renewing certificates from CAs such as Let's Encrypt made HTTPS nearly universal.

items.title: Sign
points: Transform the hash with the **private key**: that is the signature

items.title: Verify
points: Take the **public key**, the update and the signature
One changed byte, or a different key, and verification fails

visual.caption: Common algorithms: RSA signatures, ECDSA and Ed25519.

steps.label: Root CA
steps.detail: Self-signed, preinstalled in the OS or browser trust store, key kept offline

steps.label: Intermediate CA
steps.detail: Signed by the root; issues the site certificates

steps.label: Leaf: www.example.com
steps.detail: Public key, hostname and validity dates, signed by the intermediate. The server sends it with the intermediate

sections.pitfall: Clicking through a certificate warning on a site that should have a valid certificate. That warning is exactly what an on-path attacker's fake certificate looks like.

check.question: Alice signs a file. What does Bob need to verify the signature?
choices: Alice's private key, sent to him securely
His own private key and the file
A password Alice shared with him in advance
Alice's public key, the file and the signature
check.explanation: Verification uses only public information. Alice's private key stays with her, which is exactly why a valid signature proves she made it.

sections.title: Key exchange and the TLS handshake
sections.key: Diffie-Hellman lets two strangers compute a shared secret that never crosses the wire; TLS 1.3 adds a certificate signature against impostors and ephemeral keys for forward secrecy.
sections.body:
How can your browser agree on a secret AES key with a server it has never contacted, while an eavesdropper records every byte? **Diffie-Hellman key exchange**, usually pictured as mixing paint:

[[visual]]

The real mixing is modular exponentiation or elliptic-curve math (X25519 today): easy one way, infeasible to reverse. The shared secret is **never transmitted**.

Plain Diffie-Hellman proves nothing about who is on the other end. An active man-in-the-middle can run one exchange with each side and relay everything. TLS 1.3 adds the certificate:

[[visual 2]]

The Diffie-Hellman values are **ephemeral**: fresh for each connection, then deleted. So TLS 1.3 has **forward secrecy**: a server key stolen next year cannot decrypt sessions recorded today, because that key only signed handshakes.

messages.note: Same color on both sides; nobody can unmix the mixtures
Both derive session keys; the rest is encrypted

sections.pitfall: Believing the certificate's key encrypts your traffic. In TLS 1.3 it only signs the handshake; the traffic keys come from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, which is what gives forward secrecy.

check.question: In a Diffie-Hellman exchange, what actually travels over the network?
choices: Only public values; each side computes the shared secret itself
The shared secret, encrypted with the server's public key
Each side's private value, hashed for safety
Nothing; the shared secret is preinstalled on both sides
check.explanation: Each side sends a public value derived from its private one, and combining the other side's public value with your own private value gives the same secret on both ends. The secret never crosses the wire.

sections.title: Common mistakes that break cryptography
sections.key: Cryptography fails through misuse, not broken algorithms: homemade schemes, ECB, reused nonces, weak hashes or randomness, hardcoded keys, skipped certificate checks.
sections.body:
Strong algorithms rarely fail. Real systems break in how they use them, and the same mistakes recur in security reviews and breach reports:

[[visual]]

Cryptography fails silently: the code still runs and the output still looks random. Lean on well-tested libraries with safe defaults, and have security-sensitive code reviewed by someone who knows these traps.

[[code]]

visual.title: Mistakes and fixes
rows: Rolling your own cipher, protocol, or XOR "encryption"
A vetted library's high-level API
ECB, or any mode without integrity
AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305
Reusing a nonce under the same key
A fresh random nonce per message
MD5 or SHA-1 where an attacker influences the input
SHA-256 or better
Any fast hash for passwords, salted or not
Argon2id or bcrypt
Python's `random` or JavaScript's `Math.random()` for keys, tokens, salts or nonces: predictable from earlier output
`secrets` or `os.urandom`; `crypto.getRandomValues()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`
Keys hardcoded in source code or committed config
A secret manager or the environment, and rotate keys
`verify=False` or `rejectUnauthorized: false`: still encrypted, but to whoever answered, attackers included
Fix the trust store, for example point `verify` at your internal CA bundle
Comparing secrets with `==`: it stops at the first difference, and the timing leaks the secret
A constant-time comparison: `hmac.compare_digest`
Base64 or hex as "encryption"
Real encryption: encoding has no key

sections.code:
import random, secrets, hmac

# Predictable: never for tokens, keys or salts
weak = random.getrandbits(128)

# Secure: the OS's cryptographic generator
token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)

# Constant-time comparison for MAC tags and API keys
def tokens_match(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    return hmac.compare_digest(a, b)
sections.pitfall: Silencing a certificate error with verify=False during development and then shipping it. Fix the trust store instead, for example by pointing verify at your internal CA bundle.

activity.title: Encoding is not encryption
activity.prompt: Run it, then encode a secret of your own. No key appears anywhere, which is the point: HTTP Basic authentication sends exactly this kind of string, so it is only safe inside HTTPS.

props.code:
import base64

token = base64.b64encode(b"admin:hunter2").decode()
print("Looks scrambled:", token)
print("Anyone can reverse it:", base64.b64decode(token).decode())
props.task: Encode your own text, then decode it again.

check.question: Which of these makes AES-GCM encryption insecure?
choices: Using a 256-bit key
Storing the nonce next to the ciphertext
Reusing the same nonce for two messages under one key
Creating the key with AESGCM.generate_key
check.explanation: Nonce reuse under one key breaks GCM's confidentiality and lets attackers forge messages. The nonce is not secret, so storing it with the ciphertext is normal, and a 256-bit generated key is exactly right.

keyTerms.definition: Readable data before encryption, and the unreadable result after it.
Encryption where one shared secret key both encrypts and decrypts, such as AES.
Authenticated encryption, such as AES-GCM, that provides confidentiality and detects tampering.
A value used once per message with a key; it need not be secret but must never repeat.
Key pairs where the public key is shared and the private key is kept, used for encryption and signatures.
Using public-key cryptography to deliver or agree on a symmetric key that encrypts the actual data.
A one-way function mapping any input to a fixed-size digest, such as SHA-256.
A hash computed with a secret key, proving a message's integrity and origin to anyone holding the key.
A random, non-secret value unique to each password hash, so identical passwords hash differently.
A value made with a private key over a message's hash that anyone can verify with the public key.
A trusted party that signs certificates binding public keys to names, forming the chain of trust.
Past sessions stay safe even if a long-term private key leaks, thanks to ephemeral key exchange.

summary: Encryption gives confidentiality, hashes and MACs integrity, signatures authenticity; secrecy lives in the key.
AES-GCM is fast but needs a shared key; never reuse a nonce and never use ECB.
Public keys let strangers agree on keys and verify signatures; real systems then switch to AES.
Hashes are fixed-size, one-way fingerprints; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken, and HMAC adds a key.
Store passwords as salted, slow hashes (Argon2id, bcrypt), never encrypted or fast-hashed.
TLS combines ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, certificate signatures and AEAD; never disable certificate checks.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how their browser and a bank's server, which have never met, end up sharing a secret key while someone records all their traffic, and how the browser knows it is really talking to the bank.

questions.question: Bob wants anyone to be able to send him messages that only he can read. Which key do the senders encrypt with?
choices: Bob's private key
Bob's public key
Each sender's own private key
A key Bob emails to each sender
questions.explanation: Senders encrypt with Bob's public key, and only Bob's private key can decrypt the result. Bob's private key must never be shared, and emailing keys around brings back the key distribution problem.

questions.question: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography instead of just one?
questions.answer: Asymmetric cryptography solves key distribution and identity but is slow, so TLS uses it only to agree on a shared secret and to authenticate the server. The bulk data is then encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM.
questions.explanation: This hybrid design gets the best of both: public keys let strangers connect safely, and symmetric ciphers keep the connection fast.

questions.question: Which symmetric cipher is the standard choice today for encrypting bulk data? Give its three-letter acronym.
questions.explanation: AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, is used for disk encryption, TLS, VPNs and more, usually in an authenticated mode such as GCM. RSA is asymmetric, so it is not used for bulk data.

questions.question: You download an installer, and its SHA-256 hash matches the one listed on the vendor's HTTPS download page. What does that tell you?
choices: The installer is free of malware
The installer is encrypted
The installer was signed with the vendor's private key
Your copy is identical to the file the vendor hashed
questions.explanation: A matching hash means the bytes are unchanged, so the download was not corrupted or swapped in transit. It does not prove the file is safe, and a hash is not a signature, since anyone can compute one.

questions.question: How many hexadecimal characters long is a SHA-256 digest?
questions.explanation: SHA-256 outputs 256 bits. Each hex character encodes 4 bits, so 256 / 4 = 64 characters, no matter how long the input is.

questions.question: What does it mean that a hash function is collision resistant?
choices: It is hard to find an input that produces one given hash
The hash cannot be turned back into the input by anyone without the key
It is hard to find any two different inputs that produce the same hash
Different inputs produce outputs of different lengths
questions.explanation: Collision resistance is about finding any matching pair. Finding an input for one given hash is preimage resistance, a different property. Hashes have no key, and their output length is always fixed.

questions.question: What does adding a unique salt to each password hash protect against?
choices: Precomputed lookup tables, and spotting users who share a password
Fast guessing, because each individual hash takes much longer to compute
Attackers reading the hashes out of the database
Users picking short or common passwords in the first place
questions.explanation: With a unique salt, identical passwords hash differently and a precomputed table would have to be rebuilt for every salt. Slowing each guess is the job of the cost factor in bcrypt or Argon2, not the salt.

questions.question: Complete the login check so it returns True only when the password is correct.
choices: hashpw
checkpw
gensalt
kdf
questions.explanation: checkpw re-hashes the attempt with the salt and cost stored in stored_hash and returns True or False. hashpw returns hash bytes, which are always truthy, so every login would pass.

questions.question: This app hashes passwords with a salt. What is the real weakness?
choices: The salt must be appended after the password, never before it
hexdigest() loses information; digest() is needed to keep every bit
SHA-256 is broken by collision attacks, so hashes can be forged
One shared salt plus a fast hash: equal passwords match and guessing is cheap
questions.explanation: A salt shared by every user means equal passwords still produce equal hashes and one cracking run covers everyone, and SHA-256 lets attackers try billions of guesses per second. SHA-256 is not broken; it is just too fast for passwords.

questions.question: Each +1 to bcrypt's cost factor doubles the work. If a hash takes 250 ms at cost 12, about how many milliseconds does it take at cost 14?
questions.explanation: Going from cost 12 to 14 is two doublings: 250 x 2 x 2 = 1000 ms. The same factor of 4 applies to every guess an attacker makes.

questions.question: Alice wants to sign a contract file so anyone can check it came from her. Which keys are used?
choices: Alice signs with her private key; anyone verifies with her public key
Alice signs with her public key; Bob verifies with his own private key
Alice signs with Bob's public key; Bob verifies with his private key
Alice and Bob both use one shared secret key
questions.explanation: Only Alice holds her private key, so only she can make the signature, and anyone with her public key can verify it. Encrypting with Bob's public key gives secrecy, not proof of who sent it.

questions.question: Alice digitally signs an email but does not encrypt it. Which statement is true?
choices: Only the intended recipient is able to read its contents
Nobody can read it unless they have Alice's private key
Anyone who intercepts it can read it, but edits would be detected
It can no longer be forwarded to others without breaking the signature
questions.explanation: A signature provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. The content travels in the clear; any edit would make the signature check fail.

questions.question: Your browser accepts the certificate for www.example.com without a warning. Why does it trust it?
choices: The server also sent a root certificate, which the browser accepts
It chains to a root CA in the trust store, and its name and dates check out
The certificate itself is encrypted with the site's private key
The page was loaded over port 443, which is always trusted
questions.explanation: Trust starts at a root CA that is preinstalled, then each signature down the chain is verified, along with the name, dates and revocation status. A root supplied by the server proves nothing, because an attacker could send their own.

questions.question: This script talks to an internal API over HTTPS. What is the security problem?
questions.code:
import requests

resp = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/data",
    verify=False,
)
print(resp.json())
choices: verify=False skips certificate checks, so anyone can pose as the API
HTTPS requests also need ssl=True before traffic is encrypted
verify=False only skips the hostname check; the chain is still validated
resp.json() returns encrypted data that must be decrypted first
questions.explanation: With verify=False, requests accepts any certificate, so an attacker on the network can present their own and read or alter everything. The traffic is still encrypted, but to whoever answered. Fix the trust store instead, for example by passing verify with the path to your internal CA bundle.

questions.question: Which statement about plain Diffie-Hellman key exchange is true?
choices: The shared secret is sent over the network, but encrypted
It proves the server's identity to the client on its own
It encrypts all of the application data directly
It stops eavesdroppers but not an active man-in-the-middle
questions.explanation: The secret is never sent; each side computes it from public values. Because nothing in plain Diffie-Hellman proves identity, an attacker in the middle can run separate exchanges with each side, which is why TLS adds a certificate signature.

questions.question: Why is encrypting data with AES in ECB mode a mistake?
choices: ECB only supports short 56-bit keys, which are easy to brute-force
ECB ciphertext cannot be decrypted without the plaintext
Identical plaintext blocks encrypt identically, so patterns leak
ECB is much slower than every other block cipher mode
questions.explanation: ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, so repeated content shows up as repeated ciphertext, revealing structure. AES itself is fine; the mode is the problem. Use an authenticated mode such as GCM.

questions.question: Complete the function so password reset tokens are unpredictable.
choices: random.randbytes
secrets.token_urlsafe
random.getrandbits
secrets.randbelow
questions.explanation: secrets.token_urlsafe(32) returns 32 bytes from the operating system's secure random source, encoded for URLs. The random module is predictable once an attacker sees enough output, and secrets.randbelow(32) returns a number below 32, only 32 possibilities.

questions.question: What does Kerckhoffs's principle say?
choices: Keys should be changed every time a message is sent
Every algorithm should be kept secret from attackers
A system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public
Encryption should always be combined with compression
questions.explanation: Secrecy belongs in the key, which is small and easy to replace, not in the design, which leaks eventually. That is why standard algorithms are published and studied openly.

questions.question: Match each goal to the tool that provides it.

pairs.left: Only the intended reader can see the message
Any change to the message is detected
Anyone can verify who wrote the message
Two strangers agree on a key over a public network

questions.explanation: Each tool answers one question. Real protocols such as TLS combine them: key exchange to agree on keys, signatures to prove identity, and authenticated encryption for the data.

questions.question: What is the key distribution problem in symmetric encryption?
choices: Keys are too long to type, so they are often entered wrongly
AES keys expire after a fixed number of messages
Each message needs a different algorithm as well as a key
Both sides need the same secret key, but sending it safely needs a secure channel first
questions.explanation: A shared key works only if both sides already have it, and sending it over an open network exposes it. Public-key cryptography and Diffie-Hellman were invented to break this chicken-and-egg problem.

questions.question: What is the security flaw in this encryption helper?
choices: A 256-bit key is too long for AES-GCM
Every message is encrypted with the same nonce under the same key
GCM needs associated data, so None makes it fail
AESGCM must be created once per message, not per key
questions.explanation: A GCM nonce must never repeat under one key. With a constant nonce, an attacker who sees two ciphertexts can recover information about both plaintexts and forge new messages. Use os.urandom(12) per message and store it with the ciphertext.

questions.question: Which of these is a symmetric encryption algorithm?
choices: AES
RSA
Diffie-Hellman
questions.explanation: AES uses one shared key for both directions. RSA and Ed25519 use key pairs (Ed25519 only signs), and Diffie-Hellman agrees on a key rather than encrypting anything.

questions.question: Which statements about public-key cryptography are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The public key can be shared openly with anyone
Data encrypted with someone's public key is decrypted with their private key
It is much slower than symmetric encryption such as AES
The private key can be worked out from the public key in a few days
A message signed with a private key is hidden from everyone else
questions.explanation: Public keys are meant to be shared, the pair undoes each other's work, and the math is slow, hence hybrid encryption. Deriving the private key is infeasible, and a signature proves authorship without hiding anything.

questions.question: Complete the function so it produces an HMAC-SHA256 tag of the body with a shared secret.
choices: hmac.new
hashlib.sha256
hmac.compare_digest
hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac
questions.explanation: hmac.new(key, message, digestmod) builds a keyed hash. hashlib.sha256 takes no key, compare_digest only compares two values, and pbkdf2_hmac is a password-hashing function.

questions.question: Why is MD5 unacceptable for certificate signatures, even though nobody can turn an MD5 digest back into its input?
choices: MD5 digests can be decrypted with the right key
MD5 output is too long to fit in a certificate
Attackers can craft two different inputs with the same MD5 digest
MD5 requires a salt, and certificates do not have one
questions.explanation: A signature covers the hash, so if an attacker can make a harmless document and a malicious one with the same digest, a signature on the first also fits the second. That collision attack was used to forge a CA certificate in 2008.

questions.question: Put the steps of storing and checking a password in order.
items: At sign-up, generate a random salt for the user
Hash the password and salt with a slow function such as Argon2id
Store the salt and the hash, never the password
At login, hash the attempt with the stored salt and settings
Compare the result with the stored hash
questions.explanation: The password itself is never stored. At login the same salt and work factor reproduce the same hash only if the attempt is correct. Libraries bundle these steps into hash and verify functions.

questions.question: Why should a login system hash passwords rather than encrypt them?
choices: Encryption makes the database too large to back up
Hashing is faster, which makes cracking harder
Encrypted passwords cannot be compared at login
Encryption is reversible, so whoever steals the key recovers every password
questions.explanation: The server only needs to check a password, never to read it back. A one-way hash removes the possibility of recovery, while an encryption key stored on the same servers is often stolen along with the data. And for passwords, the hash should be slow, not fast.

questions.question: When software is signed, what does the signature actually cover?
choices: A hash of the file, transformed with the signer's private key
Every byte of the file, encrypted with the public key
Only the file's name and size
A random number chosen by the certificate authority
questions.explanation: Signing a fixed-size hash is fast, and because changing any byte changes the hash, the signature still protects the whole file. Verification recomputes the hash and checks it against the signature with the public key.

questions.question: What does a browser check before trusting a website's certificate? Select all that apply.
choices: That its chain leads to a root CA in the trust store
That the name on it matches the site's hostname
That today's date is within its validity period
That it was issued in the same country as the user
That the page loads in under one second
questions.explanation: Chain, name and dates (plus revocation status) are what make a certificate trustworthy for this site right now. Country and speed play no part.

questions.question: A server uses TLS 1.3 with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman. An attacker records its traffic today and steals the server's private key next year. What can they decrypt?
choices: Everything recorded, because the private key unlocks all sessions
Only sessions from the last 24 hours before the theft
None of the recorded sessions, because their keys came from deleted ephemeral values
Only the certificates, not the data inside the sessions
questions.explanation: The long-term key only signed the handshakes. Each session key came from Diffie-Hellman values that existed only during that connection, so they cannot be rebuilt later. That property is forward secrecy, and TLS 1.3 requires it.

questions.question: Put the steps of a TLS 1.3 handshake in order.
items: ClientHello: supported ciphers and the client's key share
ServerHello: the chosen cipher and the server's key share
Certificate and CertificateVerify: the server proves it owns the key
Finished messages confirm both sides saw the same handshake
Application data flows, encrypted with the session keys
questions.explanation: Key shares come first, so both sides can derive keys after just one exchange. The server then proves its identity by signing the handshake, both sides confirm with Finished, and only then does application data flow.

questions.question: Which of these are cryptography mistakes? Select all that apply.
choices: Hardcoding an encryption key in the source code
Using random.random() to create session tokens
Storing passwords as MD5 hashes
Using AES-GCM from a well-known library
Hashing passwords with Argon2id
questions.explanation: Hardcoded keys leak with the code, the random module is predictable, and MD5 is fast and broken. A vetted AES-GCM implementation and Argon2id are exactly the recommended choices.

questions.question: A developer "protects" API tokens in a config file by Base64-encoding them. What is wrong?
choices: Base64 makes the tokens too long to use
Base64 only works on text, not on tokens
Base64 needs a key that must be rotated often
Base64 is an encoding that anyone can reverse, with no key at all
questions.explanation: Base64 is a way of writing bytes as text, nothing more. Real protection means keeping secrets out of files entirely, in a secret manager or environment variables, or encrypting them with a properly managed key.

questions.question: This webhook check computes the right HMAC. Which change makes it safe?
questions.code:
import hmac, hashlib

def is_valid(secret: bytes, body: bytes, signature: str) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return expected == signature
choices: Switch from SHA-256 to MD5 so the check runs faster
Compare with hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)
Lowercase both strings before comparing them
Compare only the first 8 characters of each tag
questions.explanation: == stops at the first differing character, so response times leak how much of a guessed tag is right, letting an attacker build a valid one piece by piece. compare_digest takes the same time no matter where the strings differ.
